newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodians spending millions on bad medicine.
newsitem.headline: Cambodians spending millions on bad medicine.

text.p: Cambodia has become a dumping ground for illegal pharmaceuticals, attracting more than half of the staggering $180 million Cambodians spend on medicines each year, Ministry of Health officials said on Wednesday.

Secretary of State for Health Dy Narongrith said drugs which were faulty or past their expiry date flowed in from neighbouring countries to be sold in hundreds of unlicensed pharmacies, which outnumbered legal shops two to one.

The expenditure, which represents more than seven times the ministry's annual budget, equates to about $18 a person per year in a country with a per capita Gross Domestic Product (GDP) of less than $300.

Cambodian doctors were too quick to prescribe medicines because it was their main source of income, said Colin Radford, coordinator of health programmes for the Adventist Development and Relief Agency Cambodia.
"Diagnostic skill is very limited across the country, so doctors will over-prescribe medicines," Radford said. "It's like using a cannon to kill a mosquito."

The Ministry of Health counted 565 illegal pharmacies in a survey in the capital Phnom Penh last week, Dy Narongrith said. There are only 200 trained pharmacists and 276 registered pharmacies in the capital.
Dy Narongrith said a newly-passed national pharmaceuticals law could help ease the problem.
The law would allow the Ministry of Health to prosecute owners of unlicensed pharmacies and impose fines of up to $20,000 and jail terms up to 10 years.
"If we allow illegal pharmacies to exist in Cambodia, we will make our people more unhealthy," Dy Narongrith said.
